claim: 50% of the 220 tested genes yielded detectable morphological profiles
source: 50% of the 220 tested genes yielded detectable morphological profiles, which grouped into biologically meaningful gene clusters consistent with known functional annotation (e.g., the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade).
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Morphological profiles grouped into biologically meaningful gene clusters consistent with known functional annotation
source: 50% of the 220 tested genes yielded detectable morphological profiles, which grouped into biologically meaningful gene clusters consistent with known functional annotation (e.g., the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through clustering analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade is an example of biologically meaningful gene clustering
source: 50% of the 220 tested genes yielded detectable morphological profiles, which grouped into biologically meaningful gene clusters consistent with known functional annotation (e.g., the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade).
evidence: This is explicitly mentioned as an example in the abstract and detailed in the Results section.

claim: TRAF2/c-REL negatively regulates YAP1/WWTR1-responsive pathways
source: This unbiased morphologic map of gene function revealed TRAF2/c-REL negative regulation of YAP1/WWTR1-responsive pathways.
evidence: This discovery is stated in the abstract and validated through multiple experimental approaches including luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The functional connectivity between the NF-κB pathway and Hippo pathway effectors was confirmed at the transcriptional level
source: We confirmed this discovery of functional connectivity between the NF-κB pathway and Hippo pathway effectors at the transcriptional level, thereby expanding knowledge of these two signaling pathways that critically regulate tumor initiation and progression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by gene expression analysis and luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: The NF-κB pathway and Hippo pathway critically regulate tumor initiation and progression
source: We confirmed this discovery of functional connectivity between the NF-κB pathway and Hippo pathway effectors at the transcriptional level, thereby expanding knowledge of these two signaling pathways that critically regulate tumor initiation and progression.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Over 30% of genes in the human genome are of unknown function
source: Over 30% of genes in the human genome are of unknown function (Leonetti et al., 2016) and even annotated genes have additional functions yet to be uncovered.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leonetti et al., 2016.

claim: Even annotated genes have additional functions yet to be uncovered
source: Over 30% of genes in the human genome are of unknown function (Leonetti et al., 2016) and even annotated genes have additional functions yet to be uncovered.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the introduction.

claim: The number of genes and variants known to be associated with most human diseases has increased dramatically
source: The number of genes and variants known to be associated with most human diseases has increased dramatically (Amberger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Amberger et al., 2015.

claim: Understanding the function of each gene and the mechanism of each allele in disease typically remains non-systematic and labor-intensive
source: Unfortunately, the next step - understanding the function of each gene and the mechanism of each allele in the disease - typically remains non-systematic and labor-intensive.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about the current state of the field.

claim: Morphological profiling data is complementary to transcriptional profiling data
source: Morphological profiling data is complementary to transcriptional profiling data (Wawer et al., 2014) and is less expensive.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wawer et al., 2014.

claim: Morphological profiling is less expensive than transcriptional profiling
source: Morphological profiling data is complementary to transcriptional profiling data (Wawer et al., 2014) and is less expensive.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between the two methods.

claim: The Cell Painting assay consists of six stains imaged in five channels revealing eight cellular components
source: This microscopy-based assay consists of six stains imaged in five channels and revealing eight cellular components: DNA, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi, cytoplasmic RNA, nucleoli, actin, and plasma membrane (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The Cell Painting assay reveals DNA, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi, cytoplasmic RNA, nucleoli, actin, and plasma membrane
source: This microscopy-based assay consists of six stains imaged in five channels and revealing eight cellular components: DNA, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi, cytoplasmic RNA, nucleoli, actin, and plasma membrane (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: U-2 OS cells were chosen for their flat morphology and previous validation in the Cell Painting assay
source: In five replicates in 384-well plate format, we infected U-2 OS cells (human bone osteosarcoma cells), chosen for their flat morphology and previous validation in the assay, with an arrayed 'reference' expression library of 323 open reading frame (ORF) constructs of partially characterized functions (Supplementary file 1A), a subset of which have been previously described (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as the rationale for cell line selection.

claim: The experiment used 323 open reading frame (ORF) constructs of partially characterized functions
source: In five replicates in 384-well plate format, we infected U-2 OS cells (human bone osteosarcoma cells), chosen for their flat morphology and previous validation in the assay, with an arrayed 'reference' expression library of 323 open reading frame (ORF) constructs of partially characterized functions (Supplementary file 1A), a subset of which have been previously described (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Results section.

claim: 220 constructs were prioritized for analysis as most closely representative of the annotated full length transcripts
source: Of these, we prioritized analysis of the 220 constructs that were most closely representative of the annotated full length transcripts (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as a selection criterion in the Results section.

claim: Morphological profiles were extracted using CellProfiler for image processing, yielding 1384 morphological features per cell
source: Morphological profiles were extracted using CellProfiler for image processing, yielding 1384 morphological features per cell, and Python/R scripts for data processing, including feature selection and dimensionality reduction (Figure 1B, and see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The computational pipeline yielded a 158-dimensional profile for each of 5 replicates for each gene or allele tested
source: This computational pipeline yielded a 158-dimensional profile for each of 5 replicates for each gene or allele tested.
evidence: This is stated as the output of the data processing pipeline.

claim: 110 out of 220 ORF constructs induced reproducible morphological profiles distinct from negative control profiles
source: Surprisingly, we found that 50% (110/220) of these ORF constructs induced reproducible morphological profiles distinct from negative control profiles (Figure 2A, and see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 96% of wild-type ORF pairs that both yielded a distinguishable phenotype showed significant correlation to each other
source: Of the 23 pairs for which both wild-type ORFs yielded a phenotype distinguishable from negative controls, 22 (~96%) of the pairs' profiles were correlated more than expected by chance (Figure 2B, the one pair not meeting that threshold was in category b), confirming that different constructs with biological similarity indeed produce similar morphological profiles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Constitutively activating alleles typically yielded a stronger phenotype than their wild-type counterparts
source: We suspected that the small number of engineered constitutively activating alleles for certain genes would, on average, yield a stronger phenotype than their wild-type counterparts. We indeed found that correlations between replicates of the constitutively activating allele were typically higher than correlations between replicates of the wild-type version of a gene (Supplementary file 1B; p-value=0.012, one-sided paired t-test).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with statistical support (p-value=0.012).

claim: Genes in pathways known to affect cellular morphology were more likely to yield a morphological phenotype distinguishable from negative controls than other genes
source: We hypothesized that genes in pathways known to affect cellular morphology (RAC1, KRAS, CDC42, RHOA, PAK1, and genes related to the Hippo pathway) would be more likely to yield a morphological phenotype distinguishable from negative controls than other genes in the analysis. Indeed, we found this to be true (Fisher's test p-value=3.7 × 10−3) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This hypothesis was tested and confirmed with statistical significance (Fisher's test p-value=3.7 × 10−3) as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The ratio of verified gene connections among the top 5% correlated gene pairs (9%) is significantly higher than that of other gene pairs (5%)
source: Indeed, looking at wild-type versions of genes showing a detectable phenotype (the 73 genes represented in the 110 constructs), the ratio of verified gene connections among the top 5% correlated gene pairs (9%, 13 verified out of 143 possible combinations) is significantly higher than that of other gene pairs (5%, 128 verified out of 2485 possible; Fisher's test p-value=0.04; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This comparison is stated with statistical support (Fisher's test p-value=0.04).

claim: 25 clusters were defined by cutting the dendrogram at a correlation level of 0.522
source: We next created a dendrogram (Figure 3) and defined 25 clusters (see Materials and methods and Figure 3—figure supplement 2) to explore the similarities among genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and the threshold is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The majority of clusters (19 out of 22 clusters containing more than one gene) were enriched for one or more Gene Ontology terms
source: After retaining only one copy of replicate ORFs, we found that the majority of clusters (19 out of the 22 clusters containing more than one gene) were enriched for one or more Gene Ontology terms (Supplementary file 1F), indicating shared biological functions within each cluster.
evidence: This is stated as a finding indicating biological meaningfulness of the clusters.

claim: Cluster 20 contains the two canonical Hippo pathway members YAP1 and WWTR1
source: First, we analyzed Cluster 20, containing the two canonical Hippo pathway members YAP1 and WWTR1 (more detail in Supplementary file 2 [PDFs A2–A20 and B2–B20 ] , and in a later section of the text).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Results section.

claim: YAP1 and WWTR1 encode core transcriptional effectors of the Hippo pathway
source: Both are known to encode core transcriptional effectors of the Hippo pathway (Johnson and Halder, 2014), and a negative regulator of these proteins, STK3 (also known as MST2), is the strongest anti-correlating gene for the cluster (Supplementary file 2 [PDF A20], panel c1).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Johnson and Halder, 2014.

claim: STK3 (also known as MST2) is a negative regulator of YAP1 and WWTR1
source: Both are known to encode core transcriptional effectors of the Hippo pathway (Johnson and Halder, 2014), and a negative regulator of these proteins, STK3 (also known as MST2), is the strongest anti-correlating gene for the cluster (Supplementary file 2 [PDF A20], panel c1).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Johnson and Halder, 2014, and supported by the morphological data showing anti-correlation.

claim: Cluster 21 is comprised of the two phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase signaling/Akt (PI3K) regulating genes, PIK3R1 and PTEN
source: Second, we noted Cluster 21 is comprised of the two phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase signaling/Akt (PI3K) regulating genes, PIK3R1 and PTEN, both frequently mutated across 12 cancer types in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) (Kandoth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citation to Kandoth et al., 2013.

claim: PIK3R1 and PTEN are both frequently mutated across 12 cancer types in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)
source: Second, we noted Cluster 21 is comprised of the two phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase signaling/Akt (PI3K) regulating genes, PIK3R1 and PTEN, both frequently mutated across 12 cancer types in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) (Kandoth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Kandoth et al., 2013.

claim: Certain isoforms of PIK3R1 reduce levels of activated Akt, a dominant negative effect
source: These results are consistent with previous observations that certain isoforms of PIK3R1 reduce levels of activated Akt, a dominant negative effect (Abell et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Abell et al., 2005.

claim: Cluster 19 includes four activators in the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade: KRAS, RAF1 (CRAF), BRAF, and MOS
source: Cluster 19 is the largest example of a tight cluster of genes already known to be associated; it includes four activators in the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade: KRAS, RAF1 (CRAF), BRAF, and MOS.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Results section.

claim: Two constitutively active alleles BRAFV600E and RAF1L613V form a separate cluster (Cluster 6) adjacent to their wild-type counterparts
source: Notably, two constitutively active alleles of these genes, BRAFV600E (Davies et al., 2002) and RAF1L613V (Wu et al., 2011), form a separate cluster (Cluster 6) adjacent to their wild-type counterparts.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Davies et al., 2002 and Wu et al., 2011.

claim: The constitutively active RAS alleles HRASG12V and KRASG12V are in Cluster 3
source: Furthermore, the constitutively active RAS alleles HRASG12V and KRASG12V (McCoy et al., 1984) are in the next-closest cluster (Cluster 3), which also contains MAP2K4 and MAP2K3 (known to be activated by Ras [Shin et al., 2005]), as well as CDKN1A (Jalili et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to McCoy et al., 1984, Shin et al., 2005, and Jalili et al., 2012.

claim: MAP2K4 and MAP2K3 are known to be activated by Ras
source: Furthermore, the constitutively active RAS alleles HRASG12V and KRASG12V (McCoy et al., 1984) are in the next-closest cluster (Cluster 3), which also contains MAP2K4 and MAP2K3 (known to be activated by Ras [Shin et al., 2005]), as well as CDKN1A (Jalili et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Shin et al., 2005.

claim: CDC42 and TRAF2 physically interact and share functions in actin remodeling
source: CDC42 and TRAF2 (Cluster 11) physically interact and share functions in actin remodeling (Marivin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Marivin et al., 2014.

claim: Deletion of CDC42 phenocopies the loss of YAP1 in kidney-specific conditional knockouts in mice
source: Confirming our approach, a functional connection between CDC42 (Cluster 11) and YAP1 (Cluster 20) has been identified: deletion of CDC42 phenocopies the loss of YAP1 in kidney-specific conditional knockouts in mice (Reginensi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Reginensi et al., 2013.

claim: The MAPK pathway activators in Cluster 19 show increased prevalence of a subpopulation of cells with strongly asymmetric ER, mitochondria, and Golgi staining, indicating a cell polarization phenotype
source: For example, the MAPK pathway activators in Cluster 19 show increased prevalence of a subpopulation of cells with strongly asymmetric ER, mitochondria, and Golgi staining, indicating a cell polarization phenotype (Figure 4C, and Supplementary file 2 [PDF 19B], Categories one and two), for which there is evidence in the literature (Samaj et al., 2004; Elsum et al., 2013; Godde et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Samaj et al., 2004, Elsum et al., 2013, and Godde et al., 2014, and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cluster 4 contains the constitutively active mutant CDC42 Q61L as well as MAP3K2 and MAP3K9
source: Cluster 4 contains the constitutively active mutant CDC42 Q61L (Nobes and Hall, 1999) as well as MAP3K2 and MAP3K9.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Nobes and Hall, 1999.

claim: Cluster 7 contains the dominant negative alleles CDC42 T17N and RAC1 T17N
source: The highly similar Cluster 7 contains the dominant negative alleles CDC42 T17N (Nobes and Hall, 1999) and RAC1 T17N (Zhang et al., 1995), a related RAS superfamily member.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Nobes and Hall, 1999 and Zhang et al., 1995.

claim: Activating and inhibiting alleles of CDC42 would yield similar phenotypes when overexpressed
source: That activating and inhibiting alleles would yield similar phenotypes when overexpressed is not surprising for CDC42 (Melendez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Melendez et al., 2011.

claim: Cluster 7 contains isoforms and alleles of AKT: specifically, AKT3 and the constitutively active E17K alleles of both AKT1 and AKT3
source: Cluster 7 also contains isoforms and alleles of AKT: specifically, AKT3 and the constitutively active E17K alleles of both AKT1 and AKT3 (Kim et al., 2008; Davies et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Kim et al., 2008 and Davies et al., 2008.

claim: Akt is essential for certain Cdc42-regulated functions
source: Akt is known to be essential for certain Cdc42-regulated functions (Higuchi et al., 2001) and vice versa (Stengel and Zheng, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Higuchi et al., 2001 and Stengel and Zheng, 2012.

claim: Cluster 11 contains the wild-type form of CDC42 as well as TRAF2
source: Finally, the nearby Cluster 11 (which is discussed in more detail later) contains the wild-type form of CDC42 as well as TRAF2, a canonical NF-κB activator; these two are known to interact and share functions in actin remodeling (Marivin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Marivin et al., 2014.

claim: Clusters 4, 7, and 11 are enriched in cells that are huge and binucleate
source: Subpopulation visualization revealed that Clusters 4, 7, and 11 are enriched in cells that are huge and binucleate (Figure 3, example images shown in Supplementary file 2 [PDF 4B]).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Genes in Clusters 4, 7, and 11 show irregularities in DNA content, including enrichment in cells with sub-2N DNA content, a decrease in cells with 2N DNA content, and a decrease in cells with S phase and 4N DNA content
source: Genes in all three clusters also show irregularities in DNA content, namely, an enrichment in cells with sub-2N DNA content, a decrease in cells with 2N DNA content, and, for most genes, a decrease in cells with S phase and 4N DNA content, indicating a significant amount of DNA fragmentation and thus apoptosis (DNA histograms in Supplementary file 2 [PDFs 4B, 7B, and 11B]).
evidence: This is stated and shown in DNA histograms in Supplementary file 2.

claim: DNA fragmentation indicates apoptosis
source: Genes in all three clusters also show irregularities in DNA content, namely, an enrichment in cells with sub-2N DNA content, a decrease in cells with 2N DNA content, and, for most genes, a decrease in cells with S phase and 4N DNA content, indicating a significant amount of DNA fragmentation and thus apoptosis (DNA histograms in Supplementary file 2 [PDFs 4B, 7B, and 11B]).
evidence: This is inferred from the DNA content patterns observed.

claim: Cluster 8 contains PRKACA and two of its known substrates: GLI1 and RHOAQ63L
source: As a second test case, we examined Cluster 8, which contains PRKACA (the catalytic subunit α of protein kinase A, PKA) and two of its known substrates: GLI1 (a transcription factor mediating Hedgehog signaling)(Asaoka, 2012), and RHOAQ63L (a Ras homolog gene family member)(Lang et al., 1996; Rolli-Derkinderen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Asaoka, 2012, Lang et al., 1996, and Rolli-Derkinderen et al., 2005.

claim: GLI1 is a transcription factor mediating Hedgehog signaling
source: As a second test case, we examined Cluster 8, which contains PRKACA (the catalytic subunit α of protein kinase A, PKA) and two of its known substrates: GLI1 (a transcription factor mediating Hedgehog signaling)(Asaoka, 2012), and RHOAQ63L (a Ras homolog gene family member)(Lang et al., 1996; Rolli-Derkinderen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Asaoka, 2012.

claim: RhoA is a known regulator of cell morphology and cell rounding is a known related phenotype
source: RhoA is a known regulator of cell morphology and cell rounding is a known related phenotype (Oishi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Oishi et al., 2012.

claim: All members of Clusters 8 and 10 significantly induce cell rounding
source: We found that indeed all members of Clusters 8 and 10 significantly induce cell rounding (Supplementary file 1H).
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Results section.

claim: The increased roundness in Clusters 8 and 10 stems from an increased proportion of telophase, anaphase, and apoptotic cells
source: Subpopulation extraction provides a satisfying biological explanation for these clusters' distinctive phenotype: the increased roundness and strong variation in intensity levels (per the Feature Grid) across the population stems from an increased proportion of telophase, anaphase, and apoptotic cells (Figure 3 and Supplementary file 2 [PDFs 8B and 10B]).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: TRAF2 is a known regulator of NF-κB signaling
source: We noticed that the known regulator of NF-κB signaling, TRAF2 (in Cluster 11, together with CDC42) (Grech et al., 2004; Tada et al., 2001), yields a signature strongly anti-correlated to YAP1/WWTR1 (Cluster 20), which encode the transcriptional effectors of the Hippo pathway, YAP (Yes-associated protein) and TAZ (Transcriptional co-activator with a PDZ-domain).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Grech et al., 2004 and Tada et al., 2001.

claim: The Hippo pathway and NF-κB signaling are critical regulators of cell survival and differentiation
source: The Hippo pathway and NF-κB signaling are critical regulators of cell survival and differentiation, and dysregulation of these pathways is implicated in a number of cancers (Varelas, 2014; Hoesel and Schmid, 2013; Tornatore et al., 2012), but we found no evidence in the literature (in particular through BioGRID) of physical interaction between the proteins encoded by Cluster 11 genes and Cluster 20 genes.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Varelas, 2014, Hoesel and Schmid, 2013, and Tornatore et al., 2012.

claim: Dysregulation of the Hippo pathway and NF-κB signaling is implicated in a number of cancers
source: The Hippo pathway and NF-κB signaling are critical regulators of cell survival and differentiation, and dysregulation of these pathways is implicated in a number of cancers (Varelas, 2014; Hoesel and Schmid, 2013; Tornatore et al., 2012), but we found no evidence in the literature (in particular through BioGRID) of physical interaction between the proteins encoded by Cluster 11 genes and Cluster 20 genes.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Varelas, 2014, Hoesel and Schmid, 2013, and Tornatore et al., 2012.

claim: There is no evidence in the literature of physical interaction between the proteins encoded by Cluster 11 genes and Cluster 20 genes
source: The Hippo pathway and NF-κB signaling are critical regulators of cell survival and differentiation, and dysregulation of these pathways is implicated in a number of cancers (Varelas, 2014; Hoesel and Schmid, 2013; Tornatore et al., 2012), but we found no evidence in the literature (in particular through BioGRID) of physical interaction between the proteins encoded by Cluster 11 genes and Cluster 20 genes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from literature search.

claim: STK3 is a core effector of the Hippo pathway which functions to restrict YAP/TAZ nuclear activity
source: Consistent with these known functions, we found that a core effector of the Hippo pathway which functions to restrict YAP/TAZ nuclear activity, STK3 (which encodes the Mst2 kinase) (Meng et al., 2016), has a morphological signature strongly anti-correlated to YAP1/WWTR1 (Supplementary file 2 [PDF 20A, panel c1]).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Meng et al., 2016.

claim: Cluster 20 (YAP1, WWTR1) is enriched for cells that are slightly large, slightly elongated, and have disjoint, bright mitochondria patterns
source: Subpopulation analysis showed that Cluster 20 (YAP1, WWTR1) is enriched for cells that are slightly large, slightly elongated, and have disjoint, bright mitochondria patterns, whereas Cluster 11 (TRAF2, CDC42) is de-enriched for those subpopulations and instead enriched for binucleate cells, very large cells, and small cells with asymmetric organelles (Figures 3, 6A and B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figures 3, 6A and B.

claim: Cluster 11 (TRAF2, CDC42) is enriched for binucleate cells, very large cells, and small cells with asymmetric organelles
source: Subpopulation analysis showed that Cluster 20 (YAP1, WWTR1) is enriched for cells that are slightly large, slightly elongated, and have disjoint, bright mitochondria patterns, whereas Cluster 11 (TRAF2, CDC42) is de-enriched for those subpopulations and instead enriched for binucleate cells, very large cells, and small cells with asymmetric organelles (Figures 3, 6A and B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figures 3, 6A and B.

claim: Co-expression of TRAF2 or C-REL with YAP or TAZ led to significantly lower reporter activity than expression of YAP or TAZ alone
source: Co-expression of the NF-κB pathway effectors TRAF2 or C-REL with YAP or TAZ led to significantly lower reporter activity than expression of YAP or TAZ alone (Figure 6D1 and D2).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 6D1 and D2.

claim: Mutants of YAP or TAZ that are insensitive to negative regulation by the Hippo pathway (YAP-5SA and TAZ-4SA) remained sensitive to suppression of transcriptional activity by TRAF2 and C-REL
source: Intriguingly, mutants of YAP or TAZ that are insensitive to negative regulation by the Hippo pathway (YAP-5SA and TAZ-4SA; [Zhao et al., 2008]) remained sensitive to suppression of transcriptional activity by TRAF2 and C-REL, indicating that the negative relationship we identified may be independent of canonical upstream Hippo pathway signals (Figure 6D3 and D4).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Zhao et al., 2008 and shown in Figure 6D3 and D4.

claim: The negative relationship between NF-κB effectors and YAP/TAZ may be independent of canonical upstream Hippo pathway signals
source: Intriguingly, mutants of YAP or TAZ that are insensitive to negative regulation by the Hippo pathway (YAP-5SA and TAZ-4SA; [Zhao et al., 2008]) remained sensitive to suppression of transcriptional activity by TRAF2 and C-REL, indicating that the negative relationship we identified may be independent of canonical upstream Hippo pathway signals (Figure 6D3 and D4).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Hippo-insensitive mutants still respond to TRAF2 and C-REL.

claim: Connections among genes can be profitably analyzed using morphological profiling of overexpressed genes via the Cell Painting assay
source: We conclude that connections among genes can be profitably analyzed using morphological profiling of overexpressed genes via the Cell Painting assay.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: Morphological data from the Cell Painting assay, together with novel subpopulation visualization methods, can be used to flesh out the functionality of particular genes and/or clusters of interest
source: Further, we found that morphological data from the Cell Painting assay, together with novel subpopulation visualization methods, can be used to flesh out the functionality of particular genes and/or clusters of interest.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: YAP/TAZ-directed transcription is negatively regulated by NF-κB pathway effectors
source: Through validation of these clustered genes, we have identified that YAP/TAZ-directed transcription is negatively regulated by NF-κB pathway effectors and our data suggests a novel regulatory mechanism that is independent of upstream Hippo kinases.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section, supported by multiple experimental validations.

claim: The regulatory mechanism between NF-κB pathway effectors and YAP/TAZ is independent of upstream Hippo kinases
source: Through validation of these clustered genes, we have identified that YAP/TAZ-directed transcription is negatively regulated by NF-κB pathway effectors and our data suggests a novel regulatory mechanism that is independent of upstream Hippo kinases.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data showing Hippo-insensitive mutants still respond to NF-κB effectors.

claim: Hippo pathway kinases, such as Mst2, may affect the NF-κB pathway through phosphorylation of IkB proteins, thereby promoting nuclear translocation of NF-κB transcription factors
source: Recent work examining osteoclast-osteoblast differentiation has suggested that Hippo pathway kinases, such as Mst2, may affect the NF-κB pathway through phosphorylation of IkB proteins, thereby promoting nuclear translocation of NF-κB transcription factors (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: TAZ is a direct target of NF-κB transcription factors and its expression is regulated via NF-κB signaling
source: TAZ was found to be a direct target of NF-κB transcription factors and its expression is regulated via NF-κB signaling (Cho et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Cho et al., 2010.

claim: In Drosophila, NF-κB activation via Toll receptor signaling negatively regulates the transcriptional activity of Yorkie through activation of canonical hippo pathway kinases
source: Recent work has demonstrated, in Drosophila, that NF-κB activation via Toll receptor signaling negatively regulates the transcriptional activity of Yorkie, the homolog of YAP/TAZ, through activation of canonical hippo pathway kinases (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: A negative regulatory relationship exists between NF-κB activation and YAP/TAZ transcriptional function in mammalian systems
source: The work described here identifies, for the first time in a mammalian system, that a negative regulatory relationship exists between NF-κB activation and YAP/TAZ transcriptional function.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding in the Discussion section.

claim: The regulation of YAP/TAZ by NF-κB occurs in a manner that is independent of Hippo pathway-mediated phosphorylation events on YAP/TAZ
source: Furthermore, we have identified that this regulation of YAP/TAZ occurs in a manner that is independent of Hippo pathway-mediated phosphorylation events on YAP/TAZ, suggesting a more direct relationship between NF-κB and YAP/TAZ signaling.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the Discussion section, based on the data with Hippo-insensitive mutants.

claim: Functionally similar genes generally yield morphologically similar cells when overexpressed
source: Our underlying hypothesis was that functionally similar genes would generally yield morphologically similar cells when overexpressed, and indeed we found this to be the case.
evidence: This is stated as the underlying hypothesis that was confirmed by the data.

claim: Gene overexpression will most commonly result in activation of the corresponding pathway via amplification of the endogenous gene's function
source: Most commonly, gene overexpression will result in activation of the corresponding pathway via amplification of the endogenous gene's function.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the Discussion.

claim: Overexpression could disrupt a protein complex, producing a trans-dominant negative effect
source: However, it is important to note that the profiling strategy to discover functional relationships does not assume or require this. For example, overexpression could also disrupt a protein complex, producing a trans-dominant negative effect that results in precisely the opposite phenotypic effect (Veitia, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Veitia, 2007.

claim: Using overexpression avoids the complications of RNAi off-target effects
source: Using overexpression avoids the complications of RNAi off-target effects (often due to seed effects), which were far more prevalent (impacting 90% of constructs in our recent study [Singh et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Singh et al., 2015.

claim: RNAi off-target effects impact 90% of constructs
source: Using overexpression avoids the complications of RNAi off-target effects (often due to seed effects), which were far more prevalent (impacting 90% of constructs in our recent study [Singh et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Singh et al., 2015.

claim: Morphological profiling can be used to predict the functional impact of disease alleles, particularly rare variants of unknown significance
source: In addition to functionally annotating genes, as demonstrated here, one particularly appealing application enables personalized medicine: it should be feasible to use morphological profiling to predict the functional impact of various disease alleles, particularly rare variants of unknown significance.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application in the Discussion.

claim: mRNA profiles have been successfully used to predict the functional impact of disease alleles
source: This has recently been successful using mRNA profiles (Berger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Berger et al., 2016.

claim: Combining mRNA profiles with morphological profiles could better predict groups of alleles of similar mechanism
source: Thus, an even more exciting prospect would be to combine mRNA profiles with morphological profiles to better predict groups of alleles of similar mechanism, and ultimately to predict effective therapeutics for each group of corresponding patients.
evidence: This is stated as a potential future application in the Discussion.

claim: ~90% of the constructs in the Reference Set induce expression of the intended gene greater than two standard deviations above the control mean
source: The Reference Set of human cDNA clones utilized here has been previously described (Kim et al., 2016); ~90% of these constructs induce expression of the intended gene greater than two standard deviations above the control mean.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Kim et al., 2016.
